content: Calcium bicarbonate, also known as calcium hydrogen carbonate (Ca(HCO3)2), is not a solid compound that can be isolated in its pure form. Instead, it exists only in aqueous solutions containing calcium ions (Ca²⁺), dissolved carbon dioxide (CO2), bicarbonate ions (HCO3⁻), and carbonate ions (CO3²⁻). These solutions are typically found in natural freshwater systems. When water comes into contact with the atmosphere, it absorbs carbon dioxide. As this water interacts with rocks and sediments, it dissolves metal ions, most commonly calcium and magnesium. Consequently, natural waters from streams, lakes, and especially wells often contain dilute solutions of these bicarbonates. Such waters, referred to as hard waters, are known to form carbonate scale deposits in pipes and boilers. Additionally, they react with soaps to produce an undesirable scum. Attempts to isolate calcium bicarbonate as a solid by evaporating its solution to dryness invariably result in the formation of solid calcium carbonate (CaCO3) instead. The reaction can be represented as follows: Ca(HCO3)2 (aqueous) → CO2 (gas) + H2O (liquid) + CaCO3 (solid). Solid bicarbonates, apart from those of alkali metals, are exceedingly rare. This reaction is crucial in the formation of speleothems, such as stalactites, stalagmites, and columns, within caves. It also plays a role in the formation of the caves themselves. When water containing dissolved carbon dioxide (including additional CO2 from soil organisms) passes through limestone or other calcium carbonate-containing minerals, it dissolves some of the calcium carbonate, enriching the water with bicarbonate ions. As this groundwater enters a cave, the excess carbon dioxide is released from the solution. This release reduces the solubility of calcium carbonate, leading to its deposition as solid formations.
